query: Which material can be used for Temperature-dependent plastic deformation behaviors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), such as equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and related single-phase materials, exhibit temperature‐dependent plastic deformation behaviors because their intrinsically distorted lattice and heterogeneous microstructure enable a diversity of deformation mechanisms that are activated differently as temperature changes.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-homogenized, single-phase solid solution with fine grain sizes and possible nano-oxide inclusions, typical of HEAs prepared by methods like selective laser melting or homogenization.
generation.intervention: Perform deformation experiments (e.g., tensile or compression tests) under a controlled series of temperatures ranging from cryogenic to elevated (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 700–800 °C, up to 1000 K).
generation.conditions: Testing under controlled mechanical loading with temperature variation to capture transitions in yielding behavior and flow stress; ensuring uniform microstructure without phase segregation or decomposition within the stability range of the HEA.
generation.structural_mediator: The random distribution of multiple principal elements produces significant lattice distortion, fine grain structures, and nano-scale oxide precipitates that mediate dislocation dynamics and twinning mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, deformation is dominated by nucleation and propagation of dislocations (and possibly stacking faults/twinning), while at elevated temperatures thermal activation facilitates additional mechanisms such as grain boundary sliding, transformation-induced plasticity, and dynamic recovery. These effects combined enable a superior trade-off between strength and ductility across a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA is expected to exhibit a decrease in yield stress with increasing temperature due to thermal activation but will maintain an adequate work-hardening rate and ductility because of the activation of additional deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning, phase transformation) that compensate for thermal softening.
generation.baseline: Mechanical response and deformation behavior measured at room temperature (around 300 K).
generation.boundary: The behavior is expected to hold within the stability limits of the single-phase HEA; outside this range (e.g., at temperatures high enough to cause phase changes or intermetallic formation), the deformation mechanisms may alter unpredictably.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details such as exact yield stress changes and contributions of distinct mechanisms (e.g., dislocation slip versus twinning) can vary with processing route, alloy composition, and degree of short-range ordering. There is also uncertainty in the interplay between nano-oxide strengthening and grain boundary effects at extreme temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples with confirmed single-phase microstructure. Subject these samples to tensile or compression tests at multiple temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 800 K, 1000 K). Perform detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM, TEM, and X-ray diffraction) before and after testing to document the active deformation mechanisms.
measurements: Yield stress and flow stress curves as a function of temperature
Work-hardening rate and elongation at break
Microstructural features such as dislocation structures, twinning, and phase transformations via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples show no significant variation in plastic deformation mechanisms with temperature (e.g., absence of expected dislocation, twinning, or phase transformation evidence) or if the mechanical properties do not change in a predictable temperature-dependent manner, then the hypothesis that HEAs exploit multiple, temperature-activated deformation mechanisms is falsified.

A representative low-magnification SEM image of the materials in its as-homogenized state is shown in Figure 3 . CrCoFeMnNi HEA exhibits coarse equiaxed grain structure usually with a grain size up to 0.1 mm after homogenisation. Many of the grains are observed to have annealing twins in a recrystallized condition. In both homogenized and non-homogenized states examined, the presence of visible pores were found; these pores appear to represent casting porosity or holes left behind from particles that were removed during the polishing stage. Also, noticeable whole particles were observed, typically found in grains. By using EDX to study a few of these particles, it was discovered that they were abundant in Cr, Mn, and O, signalling that they are oxides, possibly of type MnCr 2 O 4 (based on their EDX spectra). Given that this type of alloy has previously been reported of such inclusions, their presence is not surprising [ [37] , [38] , [39] ].

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. 3.1. Deformation Behavior of Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs

Figure 2 shows the stress–strain curves of the Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs at 77, 300, and 1000 K respectively. At 77 K, Ag NW deforms via nucleation and propagation of a partial dislocation from the free surface, leaving a stacking fault inside the NW (see Figure 3 a). As deformation continues, the stacking fault further separates into two twin boundaries, which extend and continue to grow through entire NW. The cross-section area of the NW eventually converts from (110) to (100), resulting in two peaks in the SS curve, as shown in Figure 2 a. The area between two twin boundaries is transformed as also shown in Figure 3 a between 8% to 32% elongation in the Ag NW. The phase transformation is mainly driven by the surface stresses which enable the reduction in surface energy in the nanowire. On further loading, the difference between two boundaries decreases and finally vanishes at around 50% elongation, resulting in an improved work hardening.
